summary: Describes how IP-based emergency services can handle calls from vehicles, whether triggered automatically after a crash or by a person, carrying vehicle, sensor and location data. It also registers a media type and an Emergency Call Data Type for that data.

eli5.summary: When a car has a bad accident, it dials for help and sends details such as where it is. This explains how the call and details travel.

subtitle: How a crashed car can place an IP-based emergency call that carries structured vehicle and location data to the dispatcher.

tldr.problem: Today's in-vehicle emergency systems are circuit-switched and usually pass crash data to the call taker by voice or by proprietary means, so the call taker must listen and transcribe it.
tldr.mechanism: The vehicle sends a SIP emergency call whose initial INVITE carries a standardized Vehicle Emergency Data Set (VEDS) and a capabilities block, and the PSAP can later send requests such as flashing lights or asking for fresh data.
tldr.outcome: Crash data reaches the PSAP with the call itself and can be shown to the call taker as the call appears. The RFC extends RFC 8147 (eCall) by making VEDS mandatory and the eCall data optional.

today: RFC 8148 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata says it has not been obsoleted or updated. It builds directly on RFC 8147 and RFC 7852.

sections.title: Why Vehicles Need Next-Generation Calls
sections.content:
Emergency calls made by in-vehicle systems, either automatically after a serious incident or manually by an occupant, help emergency services respond quickly. Drivers often have poor location awareness, and injured or trapped victims may not be able to call.

Deployed telematics systems are circuit-switched and have no standards-based way to hand crash data to the Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP). The data is often read out by a human advisor or by text-to-speech, or sent by a proprietary mechanism. The call taker must first realize the call is vehicle-related, then listen and transcribe.

This RFC uses the term ACN (Automatic Crash Notification) broadly, even for manually triggered calls. It describes how IETF emergency calling mechanisms provide next-generation ACN (NG-ACN). It is designed with North American requirements in mind but written generically so other regions can reuse it.
sections.eli5: Old car emergency calls make the helper write down what a voice says. The new way sends the facts along with the call, like handing over a filled-in form.

sections.title: Legacy Models and Migration
sections.content:
Legacy systems use one of three models. In the TSP model, calls go to a Telematics Service Provider, which relays data to the PSAP orally and bridges in a three-way call. In the paired model, the vehicle uses a Bluetooth-paired handset to dial the emergency number and speaks location by text-to-speech. In the direct model, the vehicle dials the PSAP itself.

In the next-generation versions, the TSP model sends standard crash data from the TSP to the PSAP, and the direct model sends it end to end. For the paired model the RFC says it is unclear what facilities exist to pass data through the handset, so manufacturers might move to the direct or TSP model.

If the call lands at a PSAP that is not NG-ACN capable, the vehicle data is ignored or never received. The vehicle or TSP can tell, because the final response lacks a metadata/control block acknowledging the data, and it then falls back to conveying the data orally as for a legacy call.
sections.eli5: There used to be three ways a car could reach help. The new way keeps those routes but adds a data packet, and if the helper's office cannot read it, the car just talks instead.

sections.title: The Vehicle Emergency Data Set
sections.content:
The Vehicle Emergency Data Set (VEDS) was developed jointly by APCO and NENA. It is an XML structure with incident information such as airbag deployment, location and compass orientation, the vehicle's spatial orientation, and sensor data that can indicate crash severity and the likelihood of severe injury. Some of it appears in U.S. field triage guidelines.

VEDS travels as a SIP body part with the media type application/EmergencyCallData.VEDS+xml. For other regions or richer data, the RFC outlines the steps: standardize a data set, register a media type, add an entry to the Emergency Call Data Types registry, and register an INFO package that can carry it.
sections.eli5: VEDS is a standard crash report form. It says things like whether airbags went off and which way the car ended up, so helpers know what to expect.

sections.title: Carrying Data in SIP
sections.content:
The mechanism comes from RFC 7852. The VEDS block is a MIME body part with a unique Content-ID, and a top-level Call-Info header with a purpose of EmergencyCallData.VEDS points to it. A metadata/control object (EmergencyCallData.Control) is carried the same way.

Both are marked By-Reference; handling=optional so a legacy element, such as a gateway to a circuit-switched network, does not reject the INVITE. The PSAP puts a metadata/control acknowledgment in the final response, never in provisional responses such as 180.

Mid-call, the PSAP can request an updated VEDS using a SIP INFO request, and the vehicle replies with another INFO. If it cannot, it sends an <ack> with success set to false and a reason. The vehicle MAY also send an unsolicited updated VEDS if its data changed, and the PSAP acknowledges it.
sections.eli5: The crash form is attached to the phone call like a letter in an envelope. The helper can later ask for a new copy, and the car can send one on its own if things change.

sections.title: Call Setup
sections.content:
The vehicle sends a SIP INVITE whose Request-URI uses urn:service:sos.ecall.automatic or urn:service:sos.ecall.manual. The same service URNs are used as for eCall, since only one of the two systems is supported in any region. The INVITE carries both crash data and capabilities data, and the vehicle typically does not do routing or location queries itself, relying on the mobile network.

Nodes along the path can recognize the call as an ACN call, and the PSAP finds its data by looking at the Call-Info purpose values that start with EmergencyCallData.

This document reuses the call setup and normative requirements of RFC 8147, except that eCall MSD support is OPTIONAL and VEDS support is REQUIRED. A call may pass through the mobile network and an ESInet and its routing proxy (ESRP) before reaching a capable PSAP.
sections.eli5: The car dials a special kind of emergency address that says it is a car calling, so the call goes to a helper who can read the car's form.

sections.title: Actions the PSAP Can Request
sections.content:
This RFC adds new action values to the control block from RFC 8147, so the PSAP can ask the vehicle to do things. Sending data (VEDS MUST be supported) is the one mandatory action. The rest are optional:

  • msg-static: show or play a predefined message, identified by int-id.
  • msg-dynamic: show or speak text in a <text> child.
  • honk: sound the horn.
  • lamp: flash, turn on or turn off a lamp.
  • enable-camera: start a one-way media stream from a camera, set up by a re-INVITE from the vehicle.
  • door-lock: lock or unlock all doors.

The vehicle lists what it supports in a <capabilities> element in the initial INVITE. It acknowledges each request, except a successful data send, with an <ack> containing an <actionResult> per request. Multiple requests with the same action MUST be in separate control body parts.
sections.eli5: The helper can ask the car to do small things, like flash its lights or unlock doors. The car tells the helper which it can do, and answers yes or no to each ask.

sections.title: Registrations and the INFO Package
sections.content:
IANA registered the media type application/EmergencyCallData.VEDS+xml and added VEDS to the Emergency Call Data Types registry. The new action values were added to the Emergency Call Action registry from RFC 8147.

Three new sub-registries were created: static messages (Specification Required, where the only initial message has ID 1 and ID 0 is reserved), vehicle lamp IDs (Expert Review) and vehicle camera IDs (Expert Review). A vehicle states the highest static message ID it supports, which implies all lower ones.

The RFC also registers the EmergencyCallData.VEDS INFO package for mid-call data. The authors compared SIP MESSAGE, OPTIONS, re-INVITE, SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY and media-plane transport and chose INFO because it is tied to the dialog. Requests are expected to be rare, and most dialogs contain none.
sections.eli5: The RFC adds new names to the official lists, like adding new labels to a filing cabinet, so everyone uses the same words for lights, cameras and messages.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The security and privacy considerations of RFC 8147 and RFC 7852 apply. Location supplied with the help of an end host may be wrong, either deliberately or because a device malfunctions.

A vehicle MAY decline any requested action, for example if it cannot verify the certificate that signed the request, and can answer with a reason such as unable or security-failure. Riskier actions, such as unlocking doors, sending an updated VEDS or enabling a camera, may be declined in a vehicle-terminated call while being carried out in a vehicle-initiated emergency call.

VEDS can contain identifying and personal data about the vehicle and owner plus location, so it must be protected from unauthorized disclosure. Camera access should only be available within an emergency call or to an emergency services provider, for example by checking a certificate issued by an emergency services registrar.
sections.eli5: The car's report has private details, so it must be kept safe. The car is also allowed to say no to a request, especially a risky one.
